questions.learningObjective: recognise a set of words built on one root as a family
questions.stem: A learner is told that a dwelling in Spanish brings a family of words with it, among them la cocina, el dormitorio, el jardín and el balcón. What makes those four a family rather than four separate items?

options.text: Each names a part of a dwelling, so one root carries a set of rooms
Each can take the same suffix to form a different kind of house
options.misconception: believes a shared suffix rather than a shared root makes a family

options.text: Each is a word that English borrowed from Spanish in modern times
options.misconception: assumes a modern direction of borrowing where none took place

options.text: Each names a room that a plan of a family home is required to have
options.misconception: takes a vocabulary family to be a set of required rooms

questions.explanation: A vocabulary family is a root plus the words built on it, and here the root is the idea of a dwelling, so each of the four names a space inside one. questions.hint: Ask what the four words have in common that a word about food does not.

questions.learningObjective: recognise a cognate whose Spanish sense is not the English one

questions.learningObjective: identify the features that hold distance in a service exchange
questions.stem: A receptionist greets a guest: 'Buenas tardes, ¿tiene usted su reserva? La habitación está preparada en el tercer piso.' What does the exchange show?

questions.learningObjective: separate a proverb's literal reading from the claim a speaker makes

Stage two: the speaker is claiming that the colleague was the wrong person to hand the difficult client to, since the saying picks a creature obviously unfit for the task and applies it to someone plainly not the right one. The literal reading is a description of a scene, and it is a perfectly good sentence; what it cannot do is make a claim, and a proverb is a claim in a fixed form. The idiomatic reading keeps the image and reaches past it to a situation, so the donkey is evidence of a mismatch rather than the subject of the sentence. That is why proverbs are learned as whole sentences with their situations attached rather than as vocabulary to be plugged into new ones.

questions.stem: Stage one: name the two ordinary words for a private car in Spain and in much of Latin America. Stage two: say which you would use with a speaker from each region, and what would happen if you used the other.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the two are el coche, which is the ordinary word across Spain, and el carro, which is the ordinary word across much of Latin America, with the machine naming the car in parts of the Caribbean. Stage two: with a speaker from Madrid I would reach for el coche without hesitating, and with a speaker from Lima or Buenos Aires I would use el carro; if I used the other one the sentence would still be understood, because both are current in their own regions, but the choice would mark me as a visitor rather than as a speaker of the local variety, and that is the whole of the consequence.

questions.explanation: The second stage is the one that shows what knowing both words is for, because the penalty for the wrong choice is small in comprehension and real in effect. Neither word is an error anywhere: a speaker from one region understands the other's word perfectly well, and the substitution is marked only by the choice and not by a mistake. That is what separates regional variation from a false friend, where a sentence built from a similar-looking word is simply wrong, and a learner who treats the two situations alike either apologises for being understood or grows relaxed about an error that has not gone anywhere.

questions.learningObjective: find a second claim and decide what should happen to the paragraph
questions.stem: A paragraph gives three reasons why a town moved its market and then adds a sentence about the buses that serve the new site. Stage one: say what the last sentence is doing. Stage two: say where it belongs, and why the position matters.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the last sentence is introducing a second claim, since a reader can disagree with the reasons for moving the market and can also disagree with the transport arrangements at the new site, and one paragraph cannot serve both. Stage two: it should open a second paragraph, either straight away or after one linking sentence, because a paragraph's job is to give a single idea enough room to be argued and the second idea needs that room just as much. The position matters because a reader who reaches the end of a paragraph has normally taken its claim as settled, so a sentence that quietly disagrees with it reads as a slip rather than as a new subject.

questions.explanation: The two stages are separate jobs, and the first one is the harder half, since a sentence introducing a new claim is usually written in the same tone as the paragraph around it and gives no sign that it has arrived from somewhere else. Detecting it means asking whether a reader could disagree with the last sentence independently of the three before it, and if the answer is yes then the paragraph is carrying two arguments. What cannot be done is leave it in place and hope the reader does not notice, because the cost of not noticing is a paragraph that closes on a claim it never made.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach why two current forms for one thing are not an error
questions.stem: A learner writes el carro in a letter to an office in Madrid and el coche in a note to a friend in Bogotá, then asks which of the two was wrong. Explain what regional variation is and what the learner should do about it.

answer.exemplar: Regional variation is the existence of two or more current forms for the same thing, each ordinary in one part of the Spanish-speaking world and merely foreign in another, and neither of them is an error anywhere. The letter and the note are therefore both correct, and the only thing the two choices report is where the writer expects the reader to be. What a learner should do is learn the form of the variety they are studying well enough to be unremarkable in it, keep the other forms recognisable so that understanding survives, and choose between them on grounds of who is listening rather than on grounds of correctness.

questions.explanation: A learner who treats variation as error will correct other people, apologise for being understood, and eventually stop saying anything at all, which is a real cost for a distinction that carries no grammatical penalty. The useful habit is to separate two things that look alike: a form that is wrong everywhere, which is an error, and a form that is current somewhere and unknown elsewhere, which is a choice. Keeping the second in a separate mental drawer is what lets a learner read a novel from one country without meeting a wall of unknown words, and it costs nothing, since the form is already known.
questions.hint: Ask what a speaker from the other region would say about the word that was chosen.
